Risk factors for the development of hyperkalemia include renal insufficiency, diabetes mellitus, and the concurrent use of potassium-sparing diuretics, potassium supplements, or potassium-containing salt substitutes. These should be used cautiously, if at all, when combined with Benazepril. 2. Persistent, nonproductive cough has been reported with all ACE inhibitors, likely due to the inhibition of endogenous bradykinin degradation. This cough typically resolves after discontinuation of therapy. 3. ACE inhibitor-induced cough should be considered in the differential diagnosis of any patient presenting with a cough. 4. In patients undergoing surgery or anesthesia with agents that induce hypotension, Benazepril blocks the formation of angiotensin II, which would otherwise occur as a compensatory response to renin release. 5. Hypotension resulting from this mechanism can be corrected by expanding the intravascular volume. 6. For oral administration of Benazepril suspension (2 mg/mL), add 75 mL of Ora-Plus® to an amber polyethylene terephthalate (PET) bottle containing fifteen 20 mg Benazepril tablets. Shake the mixture for at least 2 minutes. 7. Allow the suspension to stand for a minimum of 1 hour, then shake it again for at least 1 additional minute. 8. 9. 10. Shake the suspension well before each use. 11. Benazepril and its active metabolite, benazeprilat, are primarily excreted by the kidneys. Elderly patients, who are more likely to have reduced renal function, require careful dose selection and monitoring of renal function. 12. 13. In hypertensive patients with renal artery stenosis in a solitary kidney or bilateral renal artery stenosis, renal function should be monitored during the initial weeks of ACE inhibitor therapy. 14. Concurrent use of potassium supplements or potassium-sparing diuretics with Benazepril may affect potassium levels. Potassium levels should be monitored periodically. 15. Increased serum lithium levels and symptoms of lithium toxicity have been reported in patients receiving ACE inhibitors, including Benazepril, during lithium therapy. Lithium levels should be monitored when used concomitantly with Benazepril. 16. Rarely, diabetic patients receiving an ACE inhibitor (including Benazepril) along with insulin or oral antidiabetics may develop hypoglycemia. These patients should be informed of the potential for hypoglycemic reactions and monitored accordingly. 17. In elderly, volume-depleted, or renally compromised patients, co-administration of NSAIDs (including selective COX-2 inhibitors) with ACE inhibitors like Benazepril may lead to renal function deterioration, including acute renal failure. These effects are usually reversible, and renal function should be monitored periodically. 18. The FDA package insert for Benazepril does not provide information regarding IV compatibility. 19. Human overdoses of Benazepril have not been reported, but hypotension is likely the most common manifestation, potentially accompanied by electrolyte disturbances and renal failure. 20. Laboratory determinations of serum levels of Benazepril and its metabolites are not widely available and have no established role in overdose management. 21. There is no evidence to suggest that physiological maneuvers, such as altering urine pH, would accelerate the elimination of Benazepril or its metabolites. 22. Benazepril is only slightly dialyzable, but dialysis may be considered in overdosed patients with severely impaired renal function. 23. Angiotensin II could theoretically serve as a specific antidote in Benazepril overdose, but it is not readily available outside of specialized research facilities. 24. The hypotensive effect of Benazepril is achieved through vasodilation and effective hypovolemia. Treatment of overdose may involve infusion of normal saline solution. 25. If ingestion is recent, activated charcoal should be considered. Gastric decontamination (e.g., vomiting, gastric lavage) may be appropriate in individual cases during the early post-ingestion period. 26. 27. In cases of marked hypotension, intravenous administration of physiological saline solution is recommended. Depending on the clinical situation, vasopressors (e.g., catecholamines) may be considered. 28. The FDA package insert for Benazepril does not provide information regarding signs, symptoms, or management of chronic overdose. 29. Benazepril and its active metabolite, benazeprilat, inhibit the angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE), which catalyzes the conversion of angiotensin I to the vasoconstrictor angiotensin II. Angiotensin II also stimulates aldosterone secretion by the adrenal cortex. 30. Inhibition of ACE results in decreased plasma angiotensin II levels, leading to reduced vasopressor activity and decreased aldosterone secretion. This may cause a slight increase in serum potassium levels. 31. Hypertensive patients treated with Benazepril alone for up to 52 weeks experienced serum potassium elevations of up to 0.2 mEq/L. Patients treated with Benazepril and hydrochlorothiazide for up to 24 weeks showed no consistent changes in serum potassium levels. 32. Removal of angiotensin II's negative feedback on renin secretion leads to increased plasma renin activity. 33. In animal studies, Benazepril did not inhibit the vasopressor response to angiotensin II or interfere with the hemodynamic effects of autonomic neurotransmitters such as acetylcholine, epinephrine, and norepinephrine. 34. ACE is identical to kininase, an enzyme that degrades bradykinin. Whether increased bradykinin levels contribute to the therapeutic effects of Benazepril remains unclear. 35. 36. Benazepril hydrochloride is a white to off-white crystalline substance.
